title: In the UK, it seems everyone's an expert
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes takes aim at the habit, common in UK public debate, of treating having attended school as expertise in running one. She argues that the further commentators are from a classroom, the more certain they become, and she dissects the seductive word 'just', which erases the complexity between identifying a problem and solving it. Her move is to restore context: schools operate within legal duties, funding and staffing constraints, accountability systems and thousands of individual children, while being handed ever more social responsibilities and then blamed for teacher workload. She stresses that much of teaching's relational work is invisible and fits poorly into a spreadsheet. Crucially, she insists criticism is not the enemy and that poor teaching and weak leadership must be challenged, but distinguishes curious scrutiny from certain sneering, especially from politicians who have never led a school. She closes with a call for humility and professional respect toward those doing the hard yards.
points: Hughes argues that education is unusual in that nearly everyone believes experiencing the service confers insider knowledge, a claim no one would make about surgery or aviation.
The word 'just' is flagged as a warning sign in education debate because it strips out every complexity that teachers and leaders actually work within.
She argues it is unserious to keep expanding schools' responsibilities, from mental health to knife crime, while expressing bewilderment that teachers appear overworked.

Good criticism begins with curiosity while bad criticism heads straight for certainty; she accepts scrutiny of poor teaching and weak leadership but rejects sneering from policymakers who have never done the job.
quotes: There is a curious phenomenon in education; the further some people get from an actual classroom, the more certain they become about what should happen inside one. It’s quite remarkable.
The problem with “just” is that it removes every inconvenient complexity between identifying a problem and actually solving it. Teachers and leaders work in precisely that space.
Of course context isn't an excuse. It is, however, context. Pretending it doesn't exist doesn't make you rigorous or edgy, it makes you a hot-take merchant cosplaying as an expert.
But experience of being ‘in’ a school is not synonymous with expertise in running one. The classroom somebody remembers from 1978 is not the classroom teachers are working in now.

But there is something deeply unserious about continually expanding schools' responsibilities while simultaneously expressing bewilderment that teachers appear overworked. It is the educational equivalent of loading another six suitcases into the boot and then complaining about the suspension.
But there is an enormous difference between scrutiny and sneering. Good criticism begins with curiosity and bad criticism skips all of that and heads directly for certainty.

It is easy to devise the perfect behaviour policy when you never have to implement it. Easy to announce that schools should provide another intervention when you don't have to decide what stops happening to make room for it.
